builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
summary: This is a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for diagnosing memory inconsistency in multi-agent LLM systems; it replaces informal assumptions that delegating retrieval to workers preserves the lead agent's ability to detect factual conflicts. It costs nothing in model capacity but adds evaluation instrumentation and logging of worker-to-lead evidence flow, and the operational implication is that handoff design or claim co-location must be engineered explicitly. Adoption can fail because the findings are measured on Harvey LAB document-review tasks with three models at matched generation spend, so the specific rates may not transfer to other domains, and fixing handoffs does not guarantee detection improves in a different pipeline.
rationale: The paper supplies no deployable method, but its central finding is a cheap, directly testable design rule for any multi-agent pipeline the reader operates: conflicting evidence must reach a single worker or survive the worker-to-lead handoff.
technique: Multi-agent memory inconsistency benchmark and evidence-flow profiler

claims.statement: This is a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for diagnosing memory inconsistency in multi-agent LLM systems; it replaces informal assumptions that delegating retrieval to workers preserves the lead agent's ability to detect factual conflicts. It costs nothing in model capacity but adds evaluation instrumentation and logging of worker-to-lead evidence flow, and the operational implication is that handoff design or claim co-location must be engineered explicitly. Adoption can fail because the findings are measured on Harvey LAB document-review tasks with three models at matched generation spend, so the specific rates may not transfer to other domains, and fixing handoffs does not guarantee detection improves in a different pipeline.

Requiring delegation raises retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% versus single-agent execution, but conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%; workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and detection is higher when one worker reads both claims and lower when claims are split across workers.
